claims.text: A cash flow forecast is a financial plan that sets out the cash a business expects to receive and the cash it expects to pay out over a future period, normally month by month, together with the balance of cash it expects to hold at the end of each of those periods.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A cash inflow is money actually received by the business in a period: cash sales, payments received from credit customers, capital introduced by the owner, money borrowed, the proceeds of selling an asset, or a grant received.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A cash outflow is money actually paid out by the business in a period: payments to suppliers, wages and salaries, rent, insurance, electricity and water charges, interest, tax, repayment of borrowing, the purchase of equipment, and drawings or dividends.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A cash flow forecast is laid out with one column for each future period and five rows: total cash inflows, total cash outflows, net cash flow, opening balance and closing balance, so that the effect of each period on the cash the business holds can be read straight off the table.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A cash flow forecast shows in advance the periods in which a business expects to run short of cash, which gives it time to arrange finance, reschedule spending or change its plans before the shortage arrives rather than after it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A lender or investor considering a request for finance is likely to ask to see a cash flow forecast, because it shows when the money is needed, how much is needed, and when the business expects to be able to repay.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A cash flow forecast lets a business test a planned decision before committing to it, by rewriting the figures the decision would change and reading the new closing balances.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Comparing a cash flow forecast with what actually happened shows where the estimates were wrong and by how much, which is how a business improves its later forecasts and locates the part of its operations causing a shortage.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A business can be profitable over a period and still run short of cash within it, because profit counts a sale when it is made while a cash flow forecast counts it when the customer pays, and because spending on a non-current asset leaves the bank in full in the period it is paid for.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Every figure in a cash flow forecast is an estimate, so the forecast is no more reliable than the assumptions about sales volumes, prices, payment dates and costs that were put into it, and estimates for periods further ahead are generally less reliable than those for the next month or two.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A cash flow forecast identifies when a shortage is expected but does not explain why it arises and does not correct it. It is a warning device; the decisions that follow from the warning are separate from it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Net cash flow for a period = total cash inflows for that period - total cash outflows for that period. A positive net cash flow means more cash came in than went out over the period; a negative net cash flow means more went out than came in.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Closing balance = opening balance + net cash flow. The closing balance is the amount of cash the business expects to hold at the end of the period, and it is measured in currency.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The closing balance of one period becomes the opening balance of the next, which is why a change to any one figure carries forward into the closing balance of every period after it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A negative closing balance is a forecast that the business's bank account is overdrawn by that amount at the end of the period, so finance of at least that size - normally an agreed overdraft - has to be in place by then if the payments in that period are to be met.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Amending a cash flow forecast means changing the figures the new information affects, recalculating the net cash flow of the periods concerned, and then recalculating the opening and closing balances of every period after them.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Moving a receipt or a payment from one period to another changes the closing balances of the periods in between, but leaves the closing balance at the end of the whole span unchanged, because the same amount of cash still enters or leaves within that span.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Interpreting a cash flow forecast means reading the direction and the turning points of the closing balance across the periods - when it starts to fall, when it turns negative, how deep the worst point is and whether it recovers - rather than judging the business on any single period's figure.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The balance relationship can be rearranged to recover a missing figure: opening balance = closing balance - net cash flow, and total cash inflows = net cash flow + total cash outflows.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A negative net cash flow in a period is not the same as a loss. It means more cash left the business than entered it in that period, which can happen in a period the business traded profitably if a large payment such as equipment, tax or a loan repayment fell due in it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Only movements of cash enter a cash flow forecast. A credit sale enters in the period the customer pays rather than the period the sale is made, and the purchase of a non-current asset enters in full in the period the business pays for it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Methods of improving cash flow act in one of three places: bringing cash in sooner, delaying or reducing the cash going out, or obtaining cash from a source outside the ordinary trading cycle.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Reducing the credit period offered to customers, or chasing overdue accounts, brings forward cash from sales already made. The gain is largely one-off, because once customers have moved onto the shorter terms the monthly pattern settles again, and pressing customers may cost the business sales where competitors offer easier terms.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Debt factoring is selling trade receivables to a factor, which advances most of the invoice value immediately - commonly around 80 to 90 per cent - and keeps a fee, so the business receives less than it is owed in exchange for receiving it sooner. Under a recourse agreement the business carries the loss if the customer never pays; under a non-recourse agreement the factor carries that loss and charges more for doing so.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Taking longer to pay suppliers, or negotiating longer credit terms, keeps cash inside the business for longer at no direct interest cost. Early-settlement discounts are given up, supplier relationships can be damaged, and a supplier may respond by tightening terms or withdrawing credit altogether.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: An agreed overdraft covers a short, predictable shortage: interest is charged on the amount actually drawn, the facility can be used and repaid as needed, and the bank can usually reduce or withdraw it at short notice. A short-term bank loan, secured on an asset or unsecured, fixes the sum and the repayment schedule instead, which suits a shortage of known size and known length.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Selling an asset the business no longer needs turns it into cash without creating a repayment obligation, and sale and leaseback releases cash from an asset the business still uses by selling it and renting it back. Both raise cash once; neither adds to the cash the business generates period after period.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Leasing equipment rather than buying it outright replaces one large cash outflow with a series of smaller ones spread across the period of use, which protects the closing balance in the period the equipment is obtained. What the arrangement is worth depends on what the agreement says: whether the charge includes maintenance, whether the business can return the asset early, and who carries the loss if the asset turns out to be worth less than expected.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Holding less inventory, and postponing or scaling down planned spending on non-current assets, both cut cash outflows in the periods concerned. Cutting inventory too far risks running out of stock and losing sales, and postponing equipment can limit capacity or raise maintenance costs later.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Cutting a cost improves cash flow to the extent that the cost is actually paid in cash within the forecast period, and the improvement can be reversed where the cut reduces the sales or the output that generate the inflows.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Most methods of improving cash flow move cash between periods rather than adding to the total the business generates, so what they relieve is a temporary shortage. A shortage that persists period after period points to a problem in the business itself - prices too low, costs too high, or too little demand - which a change of timing does not fix.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Choosing between methods of improving cash flow turns on the size of the shortage, how long it is expected to last, what each method costs, how quickly it can be arranged, and what it does to relationships with customers, suppliers and lenders.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.
